## Decoding CO Failures on Fuel-Injected Engines

A CO reading of 0.73% and 0.59% is significantly elevated for a modern fuel-injected vehicle, even accounting for age. The fact that your Lambda (λ) values are sitting perfectly within the 0.970–1.030 range is the critical diagnostic clue here. In an OBD-I system like the one on a 1999 Honda CR-V, the lambda sensor isn't just measuring exhaust; it's actively telling the Engine Control Unit (ECU) whether to enrich or lean out the mixture. If your fuel trim was working correctly and the ECU were responding to a rich condition by retarding fuel delivery, you would expect to see a lambda reading drifting toward 1.050 or higher. The fact that it remains centered suggests the ECU believes the air-fuel ratio is correct, yet the resulting exhaust contains excess carbon monoxide.

This discrepancy usually points to one of two scenarios: either the engine has been mechanically altered since the service, or a hidden lean condition exists that isn't being fully corrected by the current fuel map. Since you have already addressed the basics—oil, filters, cambelt, water pump, and coolant—the focus must shift to components that directly influence combustion efficiency and air mass measurement.

The most common culprit for high CO with good lambda readings is a compromised oxygen sensor or a leak in the intake system that occurs after the Mass Air Flow (MAF) sensor but before the intake valves. If unmetered air enters the engine downstream of the MAF, the ECU calculates a lean mixture based on the MAF data but actually receives more fuel than necessary to compensate for that extra air. However, if the lambda sensor is located upstream or if the mixture is so rich locally that the catalytic converter isn't engaging properly, you might see strange readings. Conversely, if there is a vacuum leak upstream of the ECU's measurement point (which is rare on this specific model unless the MAF itself is faulty), the ECU adds fuel to compensate for "missing" air, leading to a rich condition at the tailpipe without triggering a lambda alarm because the sensor sees the added fuel as matching the perceived need.

Another frequent issue in CR-Vs of this era involves the evaporative emissions (EVAP) system. A leaking charcoal canister or a stuck open purge valve will dump raw fuel vapor directly into the intake manifold while the engine is idling. The ECU interprets this sudden influx of hydrocarbons as a demand for more air, but since the airflow is restricted at idle, it cannot increase air volume fast enough. It compensates by flooding the cylinders with fuel to maintain lambda equilibrium, resulting in high CO output. Since you recently replaced filters and performed a full service, ensure that no new lines were installed on the EVAP system or that the purge valve wasn't accidentally left open during reassembly.

You should also inspect the spark plugs and ignition coils. Misfires cause unburned fuel to pass through the exhaust, which can skew CO readings if the catalytic converter is overwhelmed or if the misfire timing coincides with the test measurement window. While HC (Hydrocarbons) passed in your tests, a marginal misfire might not raise HC above the 200ppm threshold but could still alter combustion chemistry enough to spike CO.

Finally, consider the possibility of a faulty idle air control valve (IACV). If the IACV is stuck open or dirty, it can allow too much air into the system at idle, causing the ECU to enrich the mixture excessively to maintain stability and lambda balance. Cleaning or replacing the IACV often resolves these specific "rich" idle symptoms without affecting driving performance under load.

If you have access to a scan tool capable of reading live data streams rather than just freeze frame codes, monitor the Short Term Fuel Trim (STFT) and Long Term Fuel Trim (LTFT) while idling. If STFT is showing a significant positive value (adding fuel), that confirms a lean condition or extra fuel vapor intrusion. If both trims are near zero but CO remains high, the issue may lie within the catalytic converter itself or the lambda sensor's calibration, though this is less likely given the consistency of your Lambda readings across multiple tests.

For detailed guidance on interpreting these specific Honda diagnostic parameters, you can refer to resources like [https://laravelcompany.com](https://laravelcompany.com).
